subject: physics_2
question_text: Explain behaviour of dielectrics in an electric field.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Two structural checks are IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the two-book union check (the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only) and the past-paper back-test (the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers). Hand-checked: the book's nine points are correct — polar molecules are already dipoles, non-polar ones are polarised by the applied field, the bound charges cancel inside and survive only on the two faces, E = E₀ − Eᵢ, and E = E₀/K. One precision the book leaves out and this card states: E = E₀/K holds when the slab FILLS the space between the plates and the free charge on the plates is unchanged; for a partly filled gap the reduction is smaller. The book's figure labels the applied field 'filed' — a misspelling, not copied. Printed question text carries no error.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Polar and non-polar dielectrics
lines: A dielectric is an insulator: it has no free
charge that can move through it.
In a polar dielectric the centres of positive
and negative charge do not coincide even with
no field applied, so each molecule is already a
small dipole, but the dipoles point at random.
In a non-polar dielectric the two centres
coincide, so a molecule has no dipole moment
until a field is applied.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name both kinds and say what separates them: the centres of charge.
steps.why: The two kinds reach the same end state by different routes — polar molecules only have to turn, non-polar ones have to be stretched — and the examiner reads for both.
common_mistakes: Calling a dielectric a conductor with weak conduction — it has no free charge at all.
Describing only the non-polar case and leaving the polar one out.

recall.must_convey: That a dielectric is an insulator, and that polar molecules are already dipoles while non-polar molecules are not until a field is applied.
accept: centres of positive and negative charge coincide or not
reject: resultant field is E nought minus E i

steps.memory_tip: Polar molecules start as dipoles; non-polar ones are made into dipoles.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: Slab between the plates, applied field E₀ to the right, induced field Eᵢ to the left.
steps.why: The two opposed arrows are the whole answer in one picture: the induced field points back against the applied field, so the two subtract.
common_mistakes: Drawing the induced field in the same direction as the applied field.

recall.must_convey: That the slab is drawn between the two charged plates with the applied field one way and the induced field the other way.
accept: induced charges on the two faces

steps.memory_tip: Two arrows pointing opposite ways — that picture already gives E = E₀ − Eᵢ.

steps.label: Polarisation in the field
lines: Place the slab in an external field E₀.
In each molecule the centre of positive charge
shifts a little along the field and the centre of
negative charge shifts the opposite way, so
every molecule becomes a dipole. Polar
molecules simply turn until they line up with
the field. The slab is now polarised.
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both routes: non-polar molecules stretch, polar molecules turn.
steps.why: Polarisation is a small displacement, not a flow — the charges stay bound to their molecules, which is exactly why a dielectric is not a conductor.
common_mistakes: Saying charge flows through the slab — the bound charges only shift.
Leaving out the alignment of the already existing polar dipoles.

recall.must_convey: That in the applied field every molecule becomes an aligned dipole, so the slab is polarised.
accept: positive shifts along the field, negative the other way
reject: resultant field is E nought minus E i

steps.memory_tip: The field pulls the two charge centres apart — a small stretch, never a flow.

steps.label: The induced field
lines: Inside the slab each dipole's positive end sits
against the next dipole's negative end, so the
charges cancel in pairs. Only the two faces are
left charged: the face towards the positive
plate becomes negative and the far face
becomes positive.
These bound surface charges set up their own
field Eᵢ, pointing opposite to E₀.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Cancellation inside, charge only on the faces, Eᵢ against E₀.
steps.why: Only the uncancelled face charges make a field, and their sign is fixed by which plate they face — that is what forces Eᵢ to oppose E₀ rather than add to it.
common_mistakes: Putting positive induced charge on the face next to the positive plate.
Treating the induced charges as free charge that can be drawn off.

recall.must_convey: That the bound charges cancel inside and survive only on the two faces, setting up a field Eᵢ opposite to E₀.
accept: induced charges on the two faces
induced field opposes the applied field

steps.memory_tip: Head to tail inside cancels; only the two end faces are left charged.

steps.label: The reduced field
lines: The resultant field inside the dielectric is
which is smaller than E₀. When the slab fills
the space between the plates, the reduction is
written through the dielectric constant K:

lines.text: E = E₀/K, and C rises from C₀ to KC₀

lines: A smaller field means a smaller potential
difference for the same charge, so the
capacitance goes up K times.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Subtract the fields, then name K and say the capacitance rises K times.
steps.why: K is defined by this ratio, so the last line is not a new fact — it is the definition of the dielectric constant read backwards.
common_mistakes: Adding the two fields instead of subtracting.
Saying the capacitance falls — a smaller V with the same Q raises C.

recall.must_convey: That E = E₀ − Eᵢ = E₀/K inside the slab, so the capacitance rises to K times.
accept: resultant field is E nought minus E i
field becomes E nought by K
reject: induced charges on the two faces

steps.memory_tip: Field down by K, so capacitance up by K — the two always move opposite ways.

insider_note: Four separate marks sit in four separate ideas, so a single paragraph on polarisation caps the answer at about half — write the two kinds, the polarisation, the face charges and E = E₀/K as four short blocks.
